extracted.intended_audience: chemical safety assessors, toxicologists, industry/regulatory professionals classifying substances and mixtures under GHS
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for classifying substances and mixtures for specific target organ toxicity following single or repeated exposure (STOT‑SE and STOT‑RE), Category 3 respiratory irritation and narcotic effects, mixture classification (including bridging and cut‑offs), and aspiration hazard criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of evidence and expert judgment (STOT classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is determined by expert judgment, on the basis of the weight of all evidence available including human incidents, epidemiology, and studies in experimental animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify relevant route(s) of exposure. Use all available evidence to substantiate specific target organ toxic effects. Positive human data predominates over animal data: when well‑substantiated human data show a specific target organ toxic effect attributable to single or repeated exposure, the substance shall be classified regardless of probable dose. In exceptional cases, expert judgment may place substances with human evidence in Category 2 when human evidence is not fully convincing for Category 1, provided animal data are consistent with Category 2.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects considered to support classification for Category 1 and 2 (single exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is supported by evidence associating single exposure to the substance with a consistent and identifiable toxic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant toxic effects in humans and/or animals include (a) morbidity from single exposure; (b) significant functional changes (more than transient) in respiratory system, central or peripheral nervous systems, other organs or systems, including CNS depression and effects on special senses (sight, hearing, smell); (c) any consistent and significant adverse change in clinical biochemistry, hematology, or urinalysis; (d) significant organ damage noted at necropsy or microscopic exam; (e) multi‑focal or diffuse necrosis, fibrosis or granuloma in vital organs with regenerative capacity; (f) morphological changes potentially reversible but indicating marked organ dysfunction; (g) evidence of appreciable cell death in vital organs incapable of regeneration. All available evidence and relevance to human health must be considered.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects considered not to support classification for Category 1 and 2 (single exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain observed effects do not by themselves justify classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include: (a) clinical observations or small changes in bodyweight gain, food or water intake that do not indicate 'significant' toxicity; (b) small or transient changes in clinical biochemistry, hematology or urinalysis of doubtful/minimal toxicological importance; (c) changes in organ weights without evidence of organ dysfunction; (d) adaptive responses not toxicologically relevant; (e) substance‑induced species‑specific mechanisms demonstrated to be not relevant for human health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance values for single‑dose exposures (Table A.8.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Dose/concentration 'guidance values' are provided for consideration of the dose/concentration which has produced significant non‑lethal toxic effects in animal single‑dose studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance ranges (examples): Oral (rat) Category 1 C ≤ 300 mg/kg; Category 2 2,000 ≥ C > 300 mg/kg. Dermal (rat or rabbit) Category 1 C ≤ 1,000 mg/kg; Category 2 2,000 ≥ C > 1,000 mg/kg. Inhalation (rat) gas Category 1 C ≤ 2,500 ppmV/4h; Category 2 20,000 ≥ C > 2,500 ppmV/4h. Guidance values are for guidance only as part of the weight‑of‑evidence approach and are not strict demarcation values. Animal data may indicate classification below or above guidance values depending on nature/severity of effects and supporting information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 3 criteria — respiratory tract irritation (single exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for classifying substances as Category 3 for respiratory tract irritation include human respiratory irritant effects that impair function, and objective measures of RTI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes localized redness, edema, pruritis and/or pain with symptoms such as cough, pain, choking, breathing difficulties. Evaluation is based primarily on human data. Subjective human observations should be supported by objective measurements (e.g., electrophysiological responses, biomarkers of inflammation). Symptoms must be typical of the exposed population and not isolated idiosyncratic or ambiguous 'irritation' reports. No validated animal tests exist specifically for RTI, but single and repeated inhalation toxicity tests can provide useful reversible clinical and histopathological information as part of a weight‑of‑evidence. Category 3 for RTI is applied only when more severe organ effects are not observed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 3 criteria — narcotic effects (single exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria for classifying substances in Category 3 for narcotic effects address central nervous system depression observed in humans or animals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Human effects include drowsiness, narcosis, reduced alertness, loss of reflexes, lack of coordination, vertigo, severe headache, nausea, reduced judgement, dizziness, irritability, fatigue, impaired memory, perception/coordination deficits, slowed reaction time, or sleepiness. Animal signs may include lethargy, lack of coordination/righting reflex, narcosis, and ataxia. If such effects are not transient, consider classification as Category 1 or 2 instead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of mixtures when complete mixture data are available
rubrics_metrics.description: When reliable and good quality evidence exists for the complete mixture (human experience or appropriate animal studies), classify the mixture by weight‑of‑evidence evaluation of these data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise care that dose, duration, observation or analysis do not render results inconclusive. Use the same criteria as for substances where applicable. Mixtures may be classified for single exposure, repeated exposure, or both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bridging principles for mixtures (when mixture data unavailable)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the mixture itself has not been tested but sufficient data exist on individual ingredients and similar tested mixtures, use bridging principles to characterize hazards of the mixture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bridging principles include: Dilution; Batching; Concentration of mixtures; Interpolation within one hazard category; Substantially similar mixtures; and Aerosols. Use these approaches when they adequately characterize the mixture hazard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ingredient‑based cut‑off values for mixtures (Categories 1 and 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: If no reliable data exist for the mixture and bridging cannot be used, classify the mixture based on classification of ingredient substances when an ingredient classified as Category 1 or 2 is present at or above specified cut‑off values (Table A.8.2 / A.9.3).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cut‑off values triggering classification of a mixture: Ingredient classified as Category 1 target organ toxicant ≥ 1.0% triggers mixture classification as Category 1; Ingredient classified as Category 2 target organ toxicant ≥ 1.0% triggers mixture classification as Category 2. Apply equally to single‑ and repeated‑dose target organ toxicants. Consider potentiation or synergistic interactions when multiple toxicants affecting more than one organ system are combined; some substances can cause toxicity at <1% when potentiated by others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category 3 ingredient additivity and cut‑off considerations for mixtures
rubrics_metrics.description: For Category 3 ingredients (respiratory tract irritation and narcotic effects), apply an additive cut‑off of 20% of all Category 3 ingredients for each hazard endpoint unless evidence indicates otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 20% additive cut‑off may be higher or lower depending on specific Category 3 ingredients and the nature of effects (e.g., RTI may not occur below certain concentrations while narcotic effects may). Expert judgment required; evaluate respiratory tract irritation and narcotic effects separately. When using additivity, 'relevant ingredients' are those present at ≥1% (w/w solids, liquids, dusts, mists, vapours; v/v gases) unless there is reason to suspect an ingredient <1% is still relevant for RTI or narcotic effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: STOT‑RE category definitions and basis for classification (repeated/prolonged exposure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Substances are classified for specific target organ toxicity — repeated exposure (STOT‑RE) into Category 1 or Category 2 based on nature and severity of effects and weight of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1: substances that have produced significant toxicity in humans, or that on the basis of animal studies can be presumed to have the potential to produce significant toxicity in humans following repeated/prolonged exposure. Basis can be (a) reliable human cases/epidemiology or (b) appropriate animal studies showing significant/severe toxic effects at generally low exposure concentrations; guidance dose/concentration values are provided (A.9.2.9). Category 2: substances presumed harmful to humans on basis of animal studies showing significant toxic effects at generally moderate exposure concentrations; exceptional cases may use human evidence to place in Category 2. Identify primary target organ/system where possible and avoid including secondary effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects considered to support classification for STOT‑RE
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification is supported by reliable evidence associating repeated exposure with a consistent and identifiable toxic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relevant toxic effects include (a) morbidity or death resulting from repeated/long‑term exposure (including via bioaccumulation); (b) significant functional changes in nervous or other organ systems including CNS depression and effects on special senses; (c) any consistent and significant adverse change in clinical biochemistry, hematology, or urinalysis; (d) significant organ damage at necropsy or microscopic exam; (e) multi‑focal or diffuse necrosis, fibrosis or granuloma formation in vital organs with regenerative capacity; (f) morphological changes potentially reversible but indicating marked organ dysfunction (e.g., severe fatty change in the liver); (g) evidence of appreciable cell death in vital organs incapable of regeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects considered not to support classification for STOT‑RE
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain observations from human or animal studies do not justify STOT‑RE classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (a) clinical observations or small changes in bodyweight gain/food/water intake that do not indicate 'significant' toxicity; (b) small/transient changes in clinical biochemistry, hematology or urinalysis of doubtful/minimal importance; (c) changes in organ weights with no evidence of dysfunction; (d) adaptive responses not considered toxicologically relevant; (e) substance‑induced species‑specific mechanisms demonstrated not relevant to humans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance values for repeated exposure (Tables A.9.1 and A.9.2) and exposure‑duration extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Dose/concentration guidance values are provided for use with 90‑day repeated‑dose animal studies to assist decisions about Category 1 vs Category 2 classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category 1 guidance (90‑day rat): Oral C ≤ 10 mg/kg bw/day; Dermal C ≤ 20 mg/kg bw/day; Inhalation gas C ≤ 50 ppmV/6h/day; Inhalation vapor C ≤ 0.2 mg/L/6h/day; Inhalation dust/mist/fume C ≤ 0.02 mg/L/6h/day. Category 2 ranges (90‑day rat) e.g., oral 10 < C ≤ 100 mg/kg/day; dermal 20 < C ≤ 200 mg/kg/day; inhalation gas 50 < C ≤ 250 ppmV/6h/day; vapor 0.2 < C ≤ 1.0 mg/L/6h/day; dust/mist/fume 0.02 < C ≤ 0.2 mg/L/6h/day. Guidance values are not strict cut‑offs and should be used as part of weight‑of‑evidence. Values refer to 90‑day rat studies; extrapolate for other durations (e.g., increase guidance by factor of three for 28‑day studies) using dose/exposure time extrapolation similar to Haber's rule on case‑by‑case basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other considerations — untested substances and SAR/analogue extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a substance has not been tested for specific target organ toxicity, classification may be based on scientifically validated structure‑activity relationships (SAR) or extrapolation from a structural analogue that has been classified, together with other supporting factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use expert judgment and substantial support such as formation of common significant metabolites. When substance characterized only by animal data, reference guidance values as part of the weight‑of‑evidence. When well‑substantiated human data become available showing specific target organ toxicity, the substance shall be classified and human data predominate regardless of probable dose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspiration hazard — definitions and classification considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Aspiration hazard refers to severe acute effects (chemical pneumonia, pulmonary injury, death) occurring after aspiration of a substance or mixture; aspiration is entry of material into the trachea/lower respiratory system directly or via vomiting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classification criteria refer to kinematic viscosity (conversion from dynamic noted). Although aspiration definition includes solids, Category 1(b) classification is intended to apply to liquid substances/mixtures only. Aspiration can occur when vomited following ingestion — labeling recommendations (e.g., induce vomiting) may need modification if aspiration hazard exists. For aerosols/mists: consider whether use may form a pool in the mouth that could be aspirated. Fine mists may not form pools; streams or coarse mists from trigger/pump sprayers may form pools and should be considered for classification.
